text: The name stuck, and it meant more than the color of the plaster.
The fair was beautiful, and the fair was an argument.
It laid the world out as a ladder.
Northern Europe and white America stood at the top, in the clean geometry of the Court of Honor.
Everyone else was sorted onto the rungs below.
And you could walk that argument from one end to the other.
West of the Court of Honor ran the Midway Plaisance, a strip about a mile long.
Frederic Ward Putnam, a Harvard ethnologist, helped organize it as a kind of living museum of peoples.
There were villages up and down it.
A German village, an Irish village, a street in Cairo with camels and dancers, a Dahomey village brought from West Africa, an encampment meant to stand for Native American life.
The idea built into the layout was that a visitor would pass these displays and read them as stages of human progress, the so-called civilized at one end and the so-called primitive at the other.
The closer a group sat to the White City, the more advanced the fair meant to call it.
The villages of Africans and Native Americans were placed at the far end.
People were recruited for small pay, shipped to Chicago, and put on view for the summer.
The science was a costume.
What it actually taught was rank.
Rising over the whole strip was the Ferris Wheel, the fair's answer to the Eiffel Tower of the Paris exposition four years before.
George Washington Gale Ferris Junior, a bridge engineer, designed it.
It stood two hundred and sixty-four feet tall, with thirty-six cars that could hold sixty people each, more than two thousand riders at once.
A turn on the wheel cost fifty cents, the same as admission to the entire fair.
About a million and a half people paid it.
The wheel rose above the villages, and the crowd looked down on both.
